What I saw

Your plants are fine. The bed just isn't finished.

Your hydrangeas and boxwoods are healthy. This is a good spot for them. It's part shade. When I came by at 1pm your house was shading the whole bed. That matters for what we put in.

Photographed on the site visit, September 2026.

Your whole property is basically three plants. Rhododendron, hydrangea, hosta, plus the boxwoods out front. They're all fine. The problem is they peak at the same time. Your color shows up in one wave in early summer and then you're done for the year. We can spread that out.

There's a lot of mulch showing. That's the biggest reason this bed looks unfinished.

One more thing about this bed. Rowayton's a walking town and you've got a sidewalk out front. People see this planting from four feet away, not from a car. That's why I'd spend the money down low, on the layers you'll be standing next to.
What I'd do

Leave the big plants alone

We could move the hydrangeas and boxwoods to line up with your porch bays. I don't think the juice is worth the squeeze.

Two reasons. Blight is a real problem here and I don't want to disturb boxwood roots if I don't have to. And moving the hydrangeas would probably cost you a bloom season.

So the big plants stay put.

This fall

Two things to do

1. Move the hostas to the fenced back yard. Late September, early October. The deer are destroying them out front. That's why they've never amounted to anything. Behind the fence they'll be twice the size in two years. Costs nothing.

2. Order daffodils and get them in, same window. This is the cheapest thing you'll ever do to this bed and it gets you a spring you don't have now. Plant them in drifts down the whole run. Don't cluster them at the ends, it reads as polka dots from the sidewalk.

We're skipping tulips. They don't come back reliably and I'm not having you replant the same bed every fall. Daffodils naturalize, they get better every year, and nothing eats them.

I've given you two daffodils to choose from

OptionBloomWhat you get
A · Narcissus 'Salome'
warmer		AprilWhite petals with an apricot cup that deepens as it opens. It's warm rather than bright and it looks good against your shingle. Pick this one if you want spring to feel soft.
B · Narcissus 'Starlight Sensation'
cleaner		AprilCreamy-white and fragrant, with up to four nodding flowers on every stem. It's the one I buy when 'Thalia' sells out, and it's better. Nothing like the yellow trumpets on every lawn in town.

Either one, 60 bulbs, six inches deep, five drifts of twelve. Order from John Scheepers or Brent & Becky's in September.

The middle layer

Here are two options

Both are happy in shade. Deer leave them alone. Neither one is wispy.

It's a real trade. The actaea flowers in early autumn and then dies back for the winter. The hellebores are evergreen and flower in February when nothing else does.

OptionSeasonWhat you get
A · Actaea simplex 'Brunette'
the flower		Sep–OctA mound of near-black, deeply cut foliage. In September, bottlebrush spires shoot four to five feet out of it, opening pink-flushed and fading to white and stand above the hydrangeas like candles. They're sweetly scented, which is worth something beside a front door. It's the most sculptural thing I can give you in shade, and it's the only plant here that isn't pink, white or green. It dies to the ground in winter.
B · Helleborus × hybridus
the evergreen		Feb–AprNodding peach cups in February on leathery evergreen leaves that hold all twelve months. It gives you a season you've never had in this bed. It sits lower than the actaea, closer to knee height, so it reads as a mass rather than a spire. Deer won't touch it.
If you want my lean. Go with the hellebores if the winter view out your front window bothers you. Go with the actaea if it doesn't. Either way you can add the other one later.
The ground layer

This is the one that makes it look finished

You have no ground cover, which is why you're seeing so much mulch. Covering that soil will do more for this bed than any flower will.

Both of these are low and tidy and happy in shade. Deer ignore them. Neither one gets away from you.

OptionSeasonWhat you get
A · Geranium 'Karmina'
the pretty one		May–JunBright magenta-purple flowers over low dense foliage that turns red in fall and holds through most of the winter. It makes a tight neat mat and it fills in fast, which is what you want when the problem is bare dirt. One note: deer will nibble this one occasionally where they leave the coarse aromatic geraniums alone.
B · Symphyotrichum cordifolium
the aster		Sep–OctClouds of pale blue-lavender stars on fine dark stems, right through September and October, when everything else in this bed has finished. It's the one blue aster that's genuinely happy in shade. The deeper purple asters all want full sun and would stretch and mildew against this wall. Looser than the geranium, so pick it if you want the bed a little softer.

Big dot means in flower. Small dot means the plant's there doing its job with foliage. The daffodils give you April, which you've never had. The ground cover carries spring into early summer. The mid-tier gives you September and October if you go with the actaea, or February if you go with the hellebores. Worth knowing: actaea plus the aster puts most of your colour in autumn, while actaea plus the geranium spreads it wider. Then your hydrangeas run July into September like they always have.

The plan

Where it all goes

Swipe the drawing sideways to see the whole bed.

What to buy

LayerQuantity and sizeNotes
Daffodils60 bulbsFive drifts of twelve, 6" deep, down the whole run. Order in September, plant by late October.
Mid-tier3 · #2 potsOne in the middle of each bay, between the ground cover and the hydrangeas. Three is enough. Both options carry a lot more visual weight than their footprint. Buy the bigger pot, both are slow starters. If you go with the actaea: it's not a garden-centre shelf plant, so Broken Arrow in Hamden or mail order, and buy it in leaf if you can because the darkness varies plant to plant.
Ground cover48 · quartsAcross the whole bed at 15" spacing, under and between the shrubs and right up to the front edge. Keep it a foot clear of the boxwood stems so air still gets to the base.
Hostasexisting · relocatedOut of the front bed and into the fenced back yard. Late September, early October.
Everything elseexisting · not movingHydrangeas, boxwoods, rhododendron and the golden mop cypress all stay put.
The containers do the seasonal color. A pair at the porch steps, planted to echo the bed instead of competing with it. Bronze and burgundy in winter as you already do, apricot and cream in spring, something warm in summer. It gives the entry a focal point so the bed doesn't have to carry it.
Care

Maintenance only three times per year

  1. Late winter. Cut the hydrangeas back to a framework. If you went with the actaea, clear last year's stems while you're in there. Fifteen minutes.
  2. June. One light trim on the boxwoods, and nothing needed on the hellebores. If you went with the geranium, shear it back by a third once it's finished flowering.
  3. Late fall. Leave the hydrangea heads standing, they're your winter picture. Leave the leaves in the bed. Only thing worth clearing is anything blown up against the skirt where it'll hold damp.
Next

What I need from you

  1. Pick a daffodil. 'Salome' for warm, 'Starlight Sensation' for creamy white. This one has a deadline. Bulbs get ordered in September and planted by late October or you lose the spring.
  2. Pick a mid-tier. Actaea for near-black foliage and autumn spires, hellebores for evergreen leaves and a February bloom.
  3. Pick a ground cover. Geranium for magenta in late spring, aster for blue in September and October.

The hostas can move either way. I'd do that whatever else you decide.
